postgresql Overview ​

What It Is ​

blendsdk/postgresql is the PostgreSQL adapter for the BlendSDK data stack. It implements the abstract database contract defined by blendsdk/dbcore on top of the pg driver and the yesql named-parameter compiler, giving Node.js applications connection pooling, safe parameterized query execution, transaction management, and fluent, type-safe statement builders for INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE — with read/SELECT construction supplied by the shared dbcore builders that the database class inherits. The package is ESM-only, written in strict TypeScript, requires Node.js 22 or later, and keeps SQL explicit: it is a typed query and connection layer, not a full ORM.

Key Features ​

  • Connection pooling — every PostgreSQLDatabase instance owns a pg.Pool; pool behavior is tunable through the optional poolConfig (max, idleTimeoutMillis, connectionTimeoutMillis).
  • Named-parameter queries — SQL uses :name placeholders that yesql compiles into positional parameters, so values are never string-interpolated into the query text (SQL-injection safe).
  • Transactions — db.withTransaction(fn) wraps fn in BEGIN/COMMIT, issues a ROLLBACK automatically when fn throws, and always releases the client back to the pool.
  • Typed statement builders — db.insert<T>(), db.update<T, F>(), and db.delete<F>() return chainable builders with .values(), .filter(), .filterByExpression(), .returning(), and terminators .execute(), .executeReturnSingle(), .executeReturnAll(), .executeReturnCount().
  • RETURNING support — writer builders retrieve affected rows with returning('*') or an explicit column list.
  • Query hooks — .beforeQuery() and .afterQuery() on builders (and beforeQuery/afterQuery options on executeQuery) transform parameters before execution and records after execution — normalization, hashing, sensitive-field masking.
  • Read queries — SELECT construction via the inherited db.from() and db.selectAll() factories: column lists, aliases, computed expressions, and expression-based WHERE clauses.
  • Validated builders — INSERT and UPDATE builders throw descriptive errors when .values() was never provided, instead of emitting invalid SQL.
  • Graceful lifecycle — disconnect(timeoutMs = 10000) shuts the pool down with a forced-release fallback; opt-in SIGINT/SIGTERM handling via enableGracefulShutdown (standalone processes only — never alongside blendsdk/webafx shutdown handling).
  • Typed results — executeQuery<R>() resolves to PostgreSQLQueryResult<R> with records, rowCount, and column fields metadata.

When To Use ​

Use blendsdk/postgresql when:

  • You are building server-side Node.js applications (HTTP APIs, workers, CLI services) that talk to PostgreSQL and want explicit, type-safe SQL rather than a heavyweight ORM.
  • You need transactional units of work with automatic commit/rollback and guaranteed connection release.
  • You want structured writes — INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE through fluent builders with filters, RETURNING, and hooks — while keeping raw executeQuery for everything else.
  • You need data-layer cross-cutting concerns: transforming inputs before they reach the database and shaping or masking outputs before they reach application code.
  • You are building within the BlendSDK ecosystem — this package is the PostgreSQL implementation of the blendsdk/dbcore contract and composes with the shared types and expression-based filters used across the stack.
  • You are building an application where a framework (for example a WebApplication from blendsdk/webafx) manages process lifecycle — in that setup, let the framework own shutdown and leave enableGracefulShutdown disabled.

Keep in mind:

  • This is not a full ORM — there is no entity mapping, relation loading, or migration tooling; SQL and schema lifecycle stay explicit.
  • It is PostgreSQL-specific — other database engines require a different implementation of the dbcore contract.

Architecture ​

blendsdk/postgresql is a thin dialect adapter: statement chaining, hooks, expression compilation, and execution flow live in the base classes of blendsdk/dbcore, while this package supplies the PostgreSQL-specific SQL generation and the concrete connection layer over pg and yesql.

text
Application code
      │
      ▼
PostgreSQLDatabase ─── extends ───▶ Database (abstract, blendsdk/dbcore)
      │                               • statement execution flow & hooks
      │                               • expression compilation & caching
      ├─ factories: insert() · update() · delete() · from() · selectAll()
      ▼
PostgreSQL statement builders  (override buildQuery() / buildParameters())
      │
      ▼
yesql (:name → positional)  ──▶  pg.Pool / PoolClient  ──▶  PostgreSQL server

Design Patterns ​

  • Adapter — PostgreSQLDatabase adapts the pg connection pool and the yesql compiler to the abstract Database contract from blendsdk/dbcore.
  • Template Method — PostgreSQLInsertStatement, PostgreSQLUpdateStatement, and PostgreSQLDeleteStatement extend the dbcore base builders and override only the protected buildQuery() / buildParameters() steps; chaining, hooks, expression caching, and the execute* terminators are inherited.
  • Builder — statements are configured fluently (.values(), .filter(), .returning(), .beforeQuery(), .afterQuery()) and finalized with an execution method.
  • Factory Method — db.insert(), db.update(), and db.delete() instantiate the matching PostgreSQL builder; db.from() and db.selectAll() come from the base class for reads.
  • Strategy — WHERE conditions are compiled by the BlendSDK expression engine into SQL fragments plus parameter maps, cached per statement so query text and parameters share a single compilation. UPDATE values and filter parameters occupy separate namespaces (v_-prefixed values vs. p1…pN filters), so they can never collide.

Layered Responsibilities ​

LayerProvided byResponsibility
Contract & execution flowblendsdk/dbcoreAbstract Database, base statement builders, hooks, execute* terminators, expression caching
PostgreSQL implementationblendsdk/postgresqlPool and transaction management, SQL/parameter generation for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE
Named-parameter compilationyesql:name placeholders → safe positional parameters
Driver & poolingpgConnections, wire protocol, FieldDef column metadata

Builder factories are declared against the blendsdk/dbcore base types; the concrete instances are the PostgreSQL-specific statement classes. Public exports from the package root are the classes PostgreSQLDatabase, PostgreSQLInsertStatement, PostgreSQLUpdateStatement, PostgreSQLDeleteStatement and the interfaces PostgreSQLConfig, PoolConfig, PostgreSQLQueryResult. Shared contract types (Database, InsertStatement, ExecuteQueryOptions, FromStatement, …) originate in blendsdk/dbcore.

Dependencies ​

  • blendsdk/expression — constructs WHERE expressions in tests (query().where(...).compile()).

Environment Requirements ​

  • Node.js >= 22.0.0.
  • ESM-only: the package exposes a single import entry (with a types condition) — there is no CommonJS require() entry point.

Depended On By ​

  • BlendSDK applications and services that target PostgreSQL use this package as their concrete database layer.
  • Web frameworks in the stack interoperate with it: a WebApplication from blendsdk/webafx can manage the database lifecycle and process shutdown, in which case enableGracefulShutdown must remain disabled to avoid competing signal handlers.
  • The package is internal to the BlendSDK monorepo (packages/postgresql); npm consumers receive it through the blendsdk umbrella distribution (MIT license, TrueSoftware B.V.).

Minimum Example ​

The following is a complete program: it creates the adapter, runs one named-parameter query, prints the result, and closes the pool.

typescript
import { PostgreSQLDatabase, PostgreSQLConfig } from 'blendsdk/postgresql';

const config: PostgreSQLConfig = {
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 5432,
  database: 'appdb',
  user: 'app',
  pass: 'secret',
};

const db = new PostgreSQLDatabase(config);

try {
  const { records, rowCount } = await db.executeQuery<{ greeting: string }>(
    'SELECT :name AS greeting',
    { name: 'world' }
  );
  console.log(records[0].greeting, rowCount);
} finally {
  await db.disconnect();
}

:name is compiled by yesql into a safe positional parameter (never interpolated into the SQL text), and the executeQuery generic types the returned records. Transactions, statement builders, and hooks are covered in the dedicated documents that follow.

postgresql Core Concepts ​

blendsdk/postgresql is a thin dialect adapter over blendsdk/dbcore: the abstract database contract, the statement-chaining API, query hooks, and expression compilation live in the core package, while this package supplies the pg-based connection layer and the PostgreSQL SQL generation for the INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE builders. This document walks through every core concept of the package — what it is, how it works, a complete example, and a reference table of its key methods and properties.

The concepts covered are:

  • PostgreSQLDatabase — the adapter and its connection pool
  • Configuration and Connection Pooling — PostgreSQLConfig and PoolConfig
  • Query Execution with Named Parameters — executeQuery() and PostgreSQLQueryResult
  • Transactions — withTransaction()
  • INSERT Statement Builder — db.insert<T>()
  • UPDATE Statement Builder — db.update<T, F>()
  • DELETE Statement Builder — db.delete<F>()
  • Query Hooks — beforeQuery and afterQuery
  • Connection Lifecycle and Graceful Shutdown — disconnect() and shutdown guards

Examples in this document are written against illustrative tables (users, accounts, sessions); each example models the columns it uses. For a feature tour, see the Overview, and for a task-oriented walkthrough, see Basic Usage.

PostgreSQLDatabase ​

What It Is ​

PostgreSQLDatabase is the entry point of the package and the only class you instantiate directly. It is the PostgreSQL implementation of the abstract Database contract from blendsdk/dbcore: one instance owns one pg.Pool and exposes query execution, transaction management, and factories for the INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE statement builders. Everything else in the package — the builders and the configuration types — exists to serve an instance of this class.

How It Works ​

  • Inheritance. PostgreSQLDatabase extends Database from blendsdk/dbcore. The base class owns the shared execution flow — parameter handling, query hooks, expression compilation and caching, and the execute* terminators on statements — while this class supplies the driver integration and the dialect-specific SQL generation.
  • Lazy construction. The constructor builds a pg.Pool from the configuration but does not open a connection. pg.Pool connects on demand, so creating an instance succeeds even when the server is unreachable; connection failures surface on the first query instead.
  • Connection handling. Every atomic operation (executeQuery() outside a transaction) acquires a client from the pool and releases it in a finally block. While a transaction is active, the pinned client stored on the protected transactionClient property is reused for every statement. See Transactions.
  • Statement factories. insert(), update(), and delete() return PostgreSQL-specific builders bound to the instance, so statements execute through its pool and participate in its current transaction. The from() and selectAll() factories for SELECT statements are inherited from the base class.
  • Shutdown guard. Once disconnect() has been called, the isShuttingDown flag rejects all further queries and transactions. See Connection Lifecycle and Graceful Shutdown.

Complete Example ​

typescript
import { PostgreSQLConfig, PostgreSQLDatabase } from 'blendsdk/postgresql';

const config: PostgreSQLConfig = {
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 5432,
  database: 'appdb',
  user: 'app',
  pass: 'secret',
};

const db = new PostgreSQLDatabase(config);

try {
  const { records, rowCount } = await db.executeQuery<{ server_time: Date }>(
    'SELECT now() AS server_time'
  );

  console.log(`Server time: ${records[0].server_time.toISOString()} (${rowCount} row)`);
} finally {
  await db.disconnect();
}

Key Methods and Properties ​

NameType / SignatureDescription
constructor(config: PostgreSQLConfig)Creates the adapter and initializes its pg.Pool from the configuration
executeQuery<R>(query: string, params?: Record<string, unknown>, options?: ExecuteQueryOptions) => Promise<PostgreSQLQueryResult<R>>Executes named-parameter SQL; see Query Execution with Named Parameters
withTransaction<T>(fn: (db: this) => Promise<T>) => Promise<T>Runs fn on a pinned client inside BEGIN/COMMIT; see Transactions
connect() => Promise<PoolClient>Acquires a raw client from the pool (used internally by transactions and atomic queries)
disconnect(timeoutMs?: number) => Promise<void>Closes the pool; the default timeout is 10 000 ms

Configuration and Connection Pooling ​

What It Is ​

PostgreSQLConfig describes everything the adapter needs to reach a server, plus optional pool tuning and lifecycle opt-ins. It extends DatabaseConfig from blendsdk/dbcore — the connection properties shared by every backend — with the PostgreSQL-specific poolConfig and enableGracefulShutdown settings. PoolConfig is the nested type that controls how the underlying pg.Pool sizes and recycles its clients.

How It Works ​

  • The constructor destructures the configuration and forwards it to pg.Pool: database, host, user, and pass (mapped to the driver's password). A port provided as a string is coerced with Number(); everything else is passed through as-is.
  • poolConfig entries are forwarded only when present. Omitted properties keep the driver defaults: max: 10, idleTimeoutMillis: 30000, and connectionTimeoutMillis: 0 (no connect timeout). Supplying no poolConfig at all is fully supported.
  • Construction validates nothing. An unreachable host or wrong credentials do not throw when the instance is created — the first query rejects instead, and disconnect() still resolves cleanly.
  • enableGracefulShutdown registers SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers that disconnect the database and exit the process (see Connection Lifecycle and Graceful Shutdown). It defaults to false.
  • ⚠️ Warning: do NOT enable enableGracefulShutdown when the database is managed by a WebApplication from blendsdk/webafx, which has its own SIGTERM/SIGINT handling. Registering both causes signal handler conflicts and unpredictable shutdown behavior. Only enable it for standalone database usage outside the web framework.

Complete Example ​

typescript
import { PostgreSQLConfig, PostgreSQLDatabase } from 'blendsdk/postgresql';

const config: PostgreSQLConfig = {
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 5432,
  database: 'appdb',
  user: 'app',
  pass: 'secret',
  poolConfig: {
    max: 20,
    idleTimeoutMillis: 60000,
    connectionTimeoutMillis: 5000,
  },
};

const db = new PostgreSQLDatabase(config);

try {
  const { records } = await db.executeQuery<{ version: string }>('SELECT version() AS version');
  console.log(records[0].version);
} finally {
  await db.disconnect();
}

A port given as a string is accepted for convenience and numerically coerced during construction:

typescript
const config: PostgreSQLConfig = {
  host: 'localhost',
  port: '5432', // coerced with Number() in the constructor
  database: 'appdb',
  user: 'app',
  pass: 'secret',
};

Key Methods and Properties ​

PostgreSQLConfig (extends DatabaseConfig):

PropertyTypeDescription
hoststringHostname of the PostgreSQL server
port?number | stringServer port; strings are coerced with Number()
databasestringName of the database to connect to
userstringDatabase role used for authentication
passstringPassword — mapped to the driver's password option
poolConfig?PoolConfigOptional connection-pool tuning (see below)
enableGracefulShutdown?booleanWhen true, registers SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers that disconnect and exit; default false

PoolConfig:

PropertyTypeDescription
max?numberMaximum number of clients in the pool (driver default: 10)
idleTimeoutMillis?numberMilliseconds a client may sit idle before being closed (driver default: 30 000)

Query Execution with Named Parameters ​

What It Is ​

executeQuery<R>() is the general-purpose execution method and the engine underneath every statement builder. SQL is written with named placeholders (:param), which the yesql compiler translates into PostgreSQL positional parameters ($1, $2, …). The generic R types the returned records, and the method resolves to a PostgreSQLQueryResult<R>.

How It Works ​

  1. Shutdown guard — rejects with Cannot execute query: database is shutting down once disconnect() has been called.
  2. Connection acquisition — if no transaction is active, a client is acquired from the pool and marked for release ("atomic" mode); inside a transaction, the pinned client is reused instead.
  3. beforeQuery hook — when provided via options, it receives the parameter map and returns the transformed one.
  4. Compilation — yesql compiles the statement: :name placeholders become $1, $2, … and the values are passed to the driver separately as positional parameters. Values are never interpolated into the SQL text, so malicious input such as ' OR 1=1 -- is treated as a literal value.
  5. Execution — the compiled text and values are sent to the client.
  6. Empty results — when rowCount === 0, the method returns { records: [], rowCount: 0, fields: [] } immediately; the afterQuery hook is not invoked.
  7. afterQuery hook — when provided, it receives the rows array and returns the transformed rows.
  8. Cleanup — in a finally block, an atomically acquired client is always released back to the pool; a failure during release is logged, never thrown.

Complete Example ​

typescript
import { PostgreSQLConfig, PostgreSQLDatabase, PostgreSQLQueryResult } from 'blendsdk/postgresql';

interface UserRow {
  id: number;
  name: string;
  active: boolean;
}

const config: PostgreSQLConfig = {
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 5432,
  database: 'appdb',
  user: 'app',
  pass: 'secret',
};

const db = new PostgreSQLDatabase(config);

try {
  const result: PostgreSQLQueryResult<UserRow> = await db.executeQuery<UserRow>(
    `SELECT id, name, active
       FROM users
      WHERE name = :name AND active = :active`,
    { name: "O'Reilly", active: true }
  );

  for (const user of result.records) {
    console.log(user.id, user.name);
  }

  console.log(`rows: ${result.rowCount}`);
  console.log(`columns: ${result.fields.map((field) => field.name).join(', ')}`);
} finally {
  await db.disconnect();
}

Key Methods and Properties ​

NameType / SignatureDescription
executeQuery<R>(query: string, params?: Record<string, unknown>, options?: ExecuteQueryOptions) => Promise<PostgreSQLQueryResult<R>>Compiles named parameters with yesql, executes the SQL, applies hooks, and returns typed records

The resolved PostgreSQLQueryResult<R> exposes:

PropertyTypeDescription
recordsR[]Rows returned by the query, typed by R
rowCountnumberNumber of rows returned (SELECT) or affected (DML)
fieldsFieldDef[]Column metadata from the pg driver — an empty array when no rows are returned

Transactions ​

What It Is ​

withTransaction<T>(fn) runs a unit of work atomically: it issues BEGIN, runs the callback, and then either COMMITs on success or ROLLBACKs on failure. The callback receives the same database instance, and every statement executed through it — raw executeQuery() calls or builder operations — runs on one pinned client, so all of them belong to the same server-side transaction.

How It Works ​

  • Shutdown guard — throws Cannot start transaction: database is shutting down if disconnect() has begun.
  • Client pinning — the first withTransaction() call acquires a client from the pool and stores it on the protected transactionClient property. The callback's argument is the instance itself (this), so the natural style is db.withTransaction(async (txDb) => { ... }) and every txDb.executeQuery(...) participates in the transaction.
  • Commit path — BEGIN is issued, fn runs, COMMIT is issued, and the callback's return value is passed through unchanged.
  • Rollback path — if fn throws, a ROLLBACK is attempted (only if COMMIT did not already succeed) and the original error is rethrown. A failing rollback is logged via console.error but never replaces the original error, so the message you see is the one your code or the server produced.
  • Guaranteed cleanup — the finally block always releases the client back to the pool and clears transactionClient, even when the rollback itself failed. A failed transaction never leaks a connection, and the instance is immediately usable again afterward.
  • Instance is busy during a transaction — because the pinned client is instance state, treat the instance as occupied while a transaction runs: use only the callback's database argument, do not start a nested withTransaction() inside the callback, and avoid firing concurrent queries on the same instance during the transaction.

Complete Example ​

typescript
import { PostgreSQLConfig, PostgreSQLDatabase } from 'blendsdk/postgresql';

interface BalanceRow {
  balance: string;
}

const config: PostgreSQLConfig = {
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 5432,
  database: 'appdb',
  user: 'app',
  pass: 'secret',
};

const db = new PostgreSQLDatabase(config);

try {
  const newBalance = await db.withTransaction(async (txDb) => {
    // Debit the source account
    await txDb.executeQuery(
      'UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - :amount WHERE id = :id',
      { amount: 100, id: 1 }
    );

    // Re-read inside the transaction to enforce the overdraft rule
    const { records } = await txDb.executeQuery<BalanceRow>(
      'SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = :id',
      { id: 1 }
    );

    if (Number(records[0].balance) < 0) {
      // Throwing rolls back the whole transaction, including the debit above
      throw new Error('insufficient funds');
    }

    // Credit the destination account
    await txDb.executeQuery(
      'UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + :amount WHERE id = :id',
      { amount: 100, id: 2 }
    );

    return records[0].balance;
  });

  console.log(`Transfer committed. New balance: ${newBalance}`);
} catch (error) {
  console.error('Transfer rolled back:', error instanceof Error ? error.message : error);
} finally {
  await db.disconnect();
}

Key Methods and Properties ​

NameType / SignatureDescription
withTransaction<T>(fn: (db: this) => Promise<T>) => Promise<T>Runs fn inside BEGIN/COMMIT; issues ROLLBACK and rethrows when fn throws; always releases the client
transactionClientPoolClient | null (protected)The client pinned while a transaction is active; null otherwise
isShuttingDownboolean (protected)Rejects new transactions once disconnect() has begun

INSERT Statement Builder ​

What It Is ​

db.insert<T>(tableName) returns a PostgreSQLInsertStatement<T> — a fluent, type-safe builder for INSERT statements. The generic T models the target row, so .values() and .returning() are checked against the table's shape. The chaining API, hooks, and execute* terminators come from the base class in blendsdk/dbcore; the PostgreSQL class overrides only the SQL and parameter generation.

How It Works ​

  • Values become columns and placeholders. Each key in .values(record) becomes a column name and its :key placeholder, producing SQL of the form INSERT INTO users (name, email) VALUES (:name, :email).
  • Parameters are the values object. buildParameters() returns the values object directly, since every key already matches its placeholder name.
  • Validated builder. Building an INSERT with no values throws — Cannot build INSERT statement for table "users": no values provided. Call .values() with at least one column before executing. — instead of emitting invalid SQL.
  • Optional RETURNING. .returning('*') or .returning([...columns]) appends a RETURNING clause, making the inserted rows available to the executeReturnSingle() / executeReturnAll() terminators.
  • Termination. Statements execute through the owning database instance (and its active transaction, if any), and builder hooks registered with beforeQuery / afterQuery are applied at execution time — see Query Hooks.

Complete Example ​

typescript
import { PostgreSQLConfig, PostgreSQLDatabase } from 'blendsdk/postgresql';

interface UserRow {
  id?: number;
  name: string;
  email: string;
  active?: boolean;
}

const config: PostgreSQLConfig = {
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 5432,
  database: 'appdb',
  user: 'app',
  pass: 'secret',
};

const db = new PostgreSQLDatabase(config);

try {
  const created = await db
    .insert<UserRow>('users')
    .values({ name: 'Ada Lovelace', email: 'ada@example.com', active: true })
    .returning('*')
    .executeReturnSingle();

  if (created) {
    console.log(`Created user ${created.id}: ${created.name} <${created.email}>`);
  }

  const insertedCount = await db
    .insert<UserRow>('users')
    .values({ name: 'Alan Turing', email: 'alan@example.com' })
    .executeReturnCount();

  console.log(`Inserted ${insertedCount} user(s)`);
} finally {
  await db.disconnect();
}

Key Methods and Properties ​

NameType / SignatureDescription
values(values: Partial<T>) => thisSets the columns and values to insert; each key becomes a :key parameter
returning(columns: '*' | Array<keyof T>) => thisAppends a RETURNING clause ('*' or an explicit column list)
beforeQuery(fn: (params: Record<string, unknown>) => Record<string, unknown>) => thisRegisters a parameter transform that runs before compilation
afterQuery(fn: (records: T[]) => T[]) => thisRegisters a result transform that runs before records are returned
execute() => Promise<QueryResult<T> | null>Executes the statement and resolves with the underlying query result (records, rowCount)
executeReturnSingle() => Promise<T | null>Resolves with the first returned row, or null when no row was returned
executeReturnAll() => Promise<T[]>Resolves with all returned rows
executeReturnCount() => Promise<number>Resolves with the number of inserted rows

UPDATE Statement Builder ​

What It Is ​

db.update<T, F>(tableName) returns a PostgreSQLUpdateStatement<T, F> — a fluent builder for UPDATE statements with a SET clause typed by T, a WHERE clause typed by F, and optional RETURNING support. It shares the chaining API, hooks, and terminators of the base builder; the PostgreSQL class supplies the dialect-specific SQL generation.

How It Works ​

  • SET clause with a dedicated parameter namespace. Each key in .values(record) produces column = :v_column, so a column named active updates through :v_active.
  • WHERE clause from compiled filters. .filter({ id: 1 }) compiles the filter object into a parameterized condition through the BlendSDK expression engine (for example WHERE id = :p1), and multiple keys are joined with AND (WHERE active = :p1 AND age = :p2). The .filterByExpression() variant compiles a callback-built condition instead. The compiled expression is cached per statement, so query text and parameters never compile twice.
  • No name collisions. Values use the v_ prefix and filter parameters use p1…pN, so updating and filtering on the same column (.values({ active: true }).filter({ active: false })) produces distinct parameters: { v_active: true, p1: false }.
  • Validated builder. Building an UPDATE with no values throws — Cannot build UPDATE statement for table "users": no values provided. Call .values() with at least one column before executing.
  • Optional WHERE. When no filter is set — or the filter object is empty — no WHERE clause is generated and every row in the table is updated.
  • Optional RETURNING. As with INSERT, .returning('*') or an explicit column list makes the updated rows available to the executeReturn* terminators.

Complete Example ​

typescript
import { PostgreSQLConfig, PostgreSQLDatabase } from 'blendsdk/postgresql';

interface UserRow {
  id?: number;
  name: string;
  email: string;
  active?: boolean;
}

interface UserFilter {
  id?: number;
  email?: string;
  active?: boolean;
}

const config: PostgreSQLConfig = {
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 5432,
  database: 'appdb',
  user: 'app',
  pass: 'secret',
};

const db = new PostgreSQLDatabase(config);

try {
  const deactivated = await db
    .update<UserRow, UserFilter>('users')
    .values({ active: false })
    .filter({ email: 'ada@example.com' })
    .returning(['id', 'email', 'active'])
    .executeReturnSingle();

  if (deactivated) {
    console.log(`Deactivated user ${deactivated.id}: ${deactivated.email}`);
  }

  const affected = await db
    .update<UserRow, UserFilter>('users')
    .values({ active: true })
    .filter({ active: false })
    .executeReturnCount();

  console.log(`Reactivated ${affected} user(s)`);
} finally {
  await db.disconnect();
}

Key Methods and Properties ​

NameType / SignatureDescription
values(values: Partial<T>) => thisSets the columns to update; each key becomes a :v_key parameter
filter(filter: F) => thisBuilds the WHERE clause from the filter object (p1…pN parameters); an empty object means no WHERE
filterByExpression(fn) => thisBuilds the WHERE clause with the BlendSDK expression API; the callback receives the expression builder for F
returning(columns: '*' | Array<keyof T>) => thisAppends a RETURNING clause ('*' or an explicit column list)
beforeQuery(fn: (params: Record<string, unknown>) => Record<string, unknown>) => thisRegisters a parameter transform (v_-prefixed values and p1…pN filters)
afterQuery(fn: (records: T[]) => T[]) => thisRegisters a result transform that runs before records are returned
execute() => Promise<QueryResult<T> | null>Executes the statement and resolves with the underlying query result
executeReturnSingle() => Promise<T | null>Resolves with the first updated row, or null when no row was updated
executeReturnAll() => Promise<T[]>Resolves with all updated rows
executeReturnCount() => Promise<number>Resolves with the number of updated rows

DELETE Statement Builder ​

What It Is ​

db.delete<F>(tableName) returns a PostgreSQLDeleteStatement<F> — a fluent builder for DELETE statements whose WHERE clause is typed by F, with optional RETURNING support. Unlike INSERT and UPDATE it has no SET clause, so it never requires values; a filter is the only input that shapes which rows are affected.

How It Works ​

  • WHERE clause from compiled filters. .filter({ id: 1 }) compiles into a parameterized condition such as WHERE id = :p1, and multiple keys are joined with AND (WHERE active = :p1 AND age = :p2). The .filterByExpression() variant compiles a callback-built condition instead. Parameters are named p1…pN and are drawn from the cached compiled expression.
  • WHERE is optional. When no filter is set — or the filter object is empty — the generated statement is a bare DELETE FROM table with no WHERE clause, which deletes every row.
  • Optional RETURNING. .returning('*') or an explicit column list appends a RETURNING clause; the executeReturnSingle() and executeReturnAll() terminators then resolve with the deleted rows, and executeReturnCount() resolves with the affected row count.

Complete Example ​

typescript
import { PostgreSQLConfig, PostgreSQLDatabase } from 'blendsdk/postgresql';

interface SessionFilter {
  user_id?: number;
  status?: string;
}

const config: PostgreSQLConfig = {
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 5432,
  database: 'appdb',
  user: 'app',
  pass: 'secret',
};

const db = new PostgreSQLDatabase(config);

try {
  const expiredCount = await db
    .delete<SessionFilter>('sessions')
    .filter({ status: 'expired' })
    .executeReturnCount();

  console.log(`Removed ${expiredCount} expired session(s)`);

  const removedForUser = await db
    .delete<SessionFilter>('sessions')
    .filter({ user_id: 42 })
    .returning(['user_id', 'status'])
    .executeReturnAll();

  for (const session of removedForUser) {
    console.log(`Removed ${session.status} session for user ${session.user_id}`);
  }
} finally {
  await db.disconnect();
}

A .filter() call with an empty object produces a full-table delete — no WHERE clause is generated:

typescript
// Deletes ALL rows: "DELETE FROM sessions"
await db.delete<SessionFilter>('sessions').filter({}).execute();

Key Methods and Properties ​

NameType / SignatureDescription
filter(filter: F) => thisBuilds the WHERE clause from the filter object (p1…pN parameters); an empty object means no WHERE (all rows)
filterByExpression(fn) => thisBuilds the WHERE clause with the BlendSDK expression API; the callback receives the expression builder for F
returning(columns: '*' | Array<keyof F>) => thisAppends a RETURNING clause ('*' or an explicit column list)
beforeQuery(fn: (params: Record<string, unknown>) => Record<string, unknown>) => thisRegisters a parameter transform over the p1…pN filter parameters
afterQuery(fn: (records: F[]) => F[]) => thisRegisters a result transform that runs before records are returned
execute() => Promise<QueryResult<F> | null>Executes the statement and resolves with the underlying query result
executeReturnSingle() => Promise<F | null>Resolves with the first deleted row, or null when no row was deleted
executeReturnAll() => Promise<F[]>Resolves with all deleted rows
executeReturnCount() => Promise<number>Resolves with the number of deleted rows

Query Hooks ​

What It Is ​

beforeQuery and afterQuery are the package's cross-cutting transformation points around execution. beforeQuery transforms the parameter map before the SQL is compiled; afterQuery transforms the result rows before they reach your code. They are available in two places: chained on any statement builder, or supplied as options to executeQuery(). Typical uses are normalizing inputs (lowercasing emails, hashing passwords), adapting TypeScript values to database formats, masking sensitive fields, and enriching rows with computed properties.

How It Works ​

  • beforeQuery(params) receives the parameter map before yesql compilation and returns the transformed map. On an INSERT the map is keyed by column name (email, password_hash); on an UPDATE, value parameters are v_-prefixed (v_email) and filter parameters are p1…pN; on a DELETE, parameters are p1…pN.
  • afterQuery(records) receives the rows array after execution and before the result is returned. In executeQuery() it is only invoked when at least one row was returned — an empty result set short-circuits before the hook runs — so it can assume a non-empty array. On builders it runs as rows are extracted by executeReturnSingle() / executeReturnAll() (and the underlying execute()).
  • Errors propagate. An exception thrown inside a hook rejects the operation exactly like a query error; inside a withTransaction() callback it triggers the automatic ROLLBACK.
  • Return new objects or mutate and return. The returned value is what the next stage uses — returning a transformed copy keeps the hook pure; mutating the argument and returning it also works.

Complete Example ​

typescript
import { PostgreSQLConfig, PostgreSQLDatabase } from 'blendsdk/postgresql';

interface UserRow {
  id?: number;
  name: string;
  email: string;
  password_hash?: string;
}

const config: PostgreSQLConfig = {
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 5432,
  database: 'appdb',
  user: 'app',
  pass: 'secret',
};

const db = new PostgreSQLDatabase(config);

try {
  const created = await db
    .insert<UserRow>('users')
    .values({ name: 'Grace Hopper', email: 'GRACE@EXAMPLE.COM', password_hash: 'plain-secret' })
    .beforeQuery((params) => {
      const transformed = { ...params };
      if (typeof transformed.email === 'string') {
        transformed.email = transformed.email.toLowerCase();
      }
      if (typeof transformed.password_hash === 'string') {
        transformed.password_hash = `hash(${transformed.password_hash})`;
      }
      return transformed;
    })
    .afterQuery((records) =>
      records.map((record) => {
        const safe = { ...record };
        delete safe.password_hash;
        return safe;
      })
    )
    .returning('*')
    .executeReturnSingle();

  if (created) {
    console.log(`Stored ${created.email} — hash hidden by the hook`);
  }
} finally {
  await db.disconnect();
}

The same transforms can be applied per call through executeQuery() options:

typescript
const result = await db.executeQuery<UserRow>(
  'SELECT id, name, email FROM users WHERE email = :email',
  { email: 'GRACE@EXAMPLE.COM' },
  {
    beforeQuery: (params) => ({ ...params, email: 'grace@example.com' }),
    afterQuery: (records) =>
      records.map((record) => ({ ...record, name: record.name.toUpperCase() })),
  }
);

Key Methods and Properties ​

NameType / SignatureDescription
builder.beforeQuery(fn: (params: Record<string, unknown>) => Record<string, unknown>) => thisRegisters a parameter transform on any statement builder; runs before yesql compilation
builder.afterQuery(fn: (records: T[]) => T[]) => thisRegisters a result transform on any statement builder; runs before executeReturn* extraction
ExecuteQueryOptions.beforeQuery(params: Record<string, unknown>) => Record<string, unknown>Per-call parameter transform passed to executeQuery()
ExecuteQueryOptions.afterQuery(records: R[]) => R[]Per-call result transform passed to executeQuery(); skipped when the query returns no rows

Connection Lifecycle and Graceful Shutdown ​

What It Is ​

The lifecycle layer is what turns a long-running process into a clean one: disconnect() closes the connection pool with a timeout-protected graceful path and a forceful fallback; the isShuttingDown flag rejects new work once shutdown begins; and the optional enableGracefulShutdown config registers process signal handlers for standalone applications.

How It Works ​

  • disconnect(timeoutMs = 10000) first sets isShuttingDown = true. From that moment, executeQuery() rejects with Cannot execute query: database is shutting down and withTransaction() rejects with Cannot start transaction: database is shutting down. It is safe to call on an instance that never executed a query.
  • Graceful path with a hard ceiling. disconnect() races pool.end() against a timer. If the pool drains in time, its timer is cleared and the method resolves. If the timeout expires first, the forceful fallback runs: every pooled client is released with the driver's force flag (interrupting active queries if necessary) and the pool's internal client list is cleared, after which disconnect() resolves rather than rejecting. If ending the pool itself fails before the timeout, the error is rethrown.
  • The forceful fallback is a last resort. Releasing clients forcefully may interrupt in-flight queries and transactions; the graceful path is designed to finish well within the default 10-second ceiling for a correctly written application.
  • enableGracefulShutdown (opt-in). When enabled, the constructor registers SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that log the signal, call disconnect(), and exit the process (0 on success, 1 on failure). Leave it disabled when a framework such as blendsdk/webafx owns process shutdown — two sets of signal handlers conflict and produce unpredictable shutdown behavior. See Configuration and Connection Pooling.

Complete Example ​

typescript
import { PostgreSQLConfig, PostgreSQLDatabase } from 'blendsdk/postgresql';

const config: PostgreSQLConfig = {
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 5432,
  database: 'appdb',
  user: 'app',
  pass: 'secret',
};

const db = new PostgreSQLDatabase(config);

await db.executeQuery('SELECT 1');

// Graceful shutdown with a 5-second ceiling; forced release afterwards if needed
await db.disconnect(5000);
console.log('Pool closed');

// Any operation after disconnect is rejected by the shutdown guard
try {
  await db.executeQuery('SELECT 1');
} catch (error) {
  if (error instanceof Error) {
    console.error(error.message); // "Cannot execute query: database is shutting down"
  }
}

For standalone processes — never alongside a WebApplication from blendsdk/webafx — shutdown can be delegated to the adapter itself:

typescript
const db = new PostgreSQLDatabase({
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 5432,
  database: 'appdb',
  user: 'app',
  pass: 'secret',
  enableGracefulShutdown: true, // registers SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers
});

Key Methods and Properties ​

NameType / SignatureDescription
disconnect(timeoutMs?: number) => Promise<void>Sets isShuttingDown, ends the pool, and force-releases clients if the timeout (default 10 000 ms) expires
isShuttingDownboolean (protected)Blocks new queries and transactions while true
forceDisconnect() => Promise<void> (protected)Last-resort fallback that releases every pooled client with the driver's force flag and clears the internal client list
registerShutdownHandlers() => void (protected)Wires SIGINT/SIGTERM → disconnect() → process.exit() when enabled
enableGracefulShutdownboolean (config, default false)Opt-in process signal handling for standalone usage outside of the web framework

postgresql Basic Usage ​

This guide takes you from installing the package to running queries, transactions, and statement builders — each step adding exactly one new concept to the previous one.

Installation ​

Install the package with your preferred package manager:

npm

bash
npm install blendsdk

yarn

bash
yarn add blendsdk

pnpm

bash
pnpm add blendsdk

The runtime dependencies — blendsdk/dbcore, pg, and yesql — are installed automatically; there are no peer dependencies to add manually.

Requirements:

  • Node.js >= 22.0.0.
  • ESM only: the package exposes a single ESM entry point, so use import syntax — require() is not supported.
  • TypeScript in strict mode is recommended; the package ships its own type declarations.

Working inside the BlendSDK monorepo? Repository scripts use pnpm:

  • pnpm --filter blendsdk/postgresql build — compile the package with tsc.
  • pnpm --filter blendsdk/postgresql test — run the Vitest suite (manages a Docker-based PostgreSQL instance automatically).

Quick Start ​

The minimal setup creates the adapter, runs one named-parameter query, and closes the pool:

typescript
import { PostgreSQLDatabase } from 'blendsdk/postgresql';

const db = new PostgreSQLDatabase({
  host: 'localhost', port: 5432, database: 'appdb', user: 'app', pass: 'secret',
});

const { records } = await db.executeQuery<{ answer: number }>(
  'SELECT :a::integer + :b::integer AS answer', { a: 40, b: 2 }
);
console.log(`answer = ${records[0].answer}`); // answer = 42
await db.disconnect();

Prerequisites: a reachable PostgreSQL server and a database matching the configured credentials. This snippet skips try/finally for brevity — in real code always close the pool. Each part is explained in the sections below.

Fundamentals ​

The API is built in three layers: a database instance that owns the connection pool and executes queries, statement builders that construct structured statements, and hooks that transform parameters and results. The subsections below introduce one concept at a time.

The examples assume a reachable PostgreSQL server and three illustrative tables — users (id, name, email, active, age, password_hash), accounts (id, balance), and sessions (user_id, status). Model the columns you use with small local interfaces, as shown; adapt the names to your own schema.

Creating a Database Instance ​

PostgreSQLDatabase is the single entry point. Constructing it creates the adapter together with its pg.Pool; no connection is opened until the pool is first used, so the constructor succeeds even when the server is temporarily unreachable — the failure surfaces on the first query instead.

typescript
import { PostgreSQLConfig, PostgreSQLDatabase } from 'blendsdk/postgresql';

const config: PostgreSQLConfig = {
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 5432,
  database: 'appdb',
  user: 'app',
  pass: 'secret',
};

// Creates the adapter and its connection pool — no connection is opened yet
const db = new PostgreSQLDatabase(config);

// The pool connects on first use and is closed here
await db.disconnect();

The port also accepts a numeric string — useful when reading configuration from environment variables:

typescript
const db = new PostgreSQLDatabase({
  host: 'localhost',
  port: '5432', // coerced to 5432 with Number() in the constructor
  database: 'appdb',
  user: 'app',
  pass: 'secret',
});

Running Your First Query ​

executeQuery() runs any SQL and returns the result. Statements are written with named placeholders (:name), which the yesql compiler translates into safe positional parameters — values are never concatenated into the query text.

typescript
import { PostgreSQLDatabase } from 'blendsdk/postgresql';

const db = new PostgreSQLDatabase({
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 5432,
  database: 'appdb',
  user: 'app',
  pass: 'secret',
});

try {
  const { records } = await db.executeQuery<{ greeting: string }>(
    'SELECT :name AS greeting',
    { name: 'world' }
  );

  console.log(records[0].greeting); // world
} finally {
  await db.disconnect();
}

The generic parameter types the returned rows — records[0].greeting is a string. Queries with several parameters follow the same pattern; the local interface describes the rows you expect back:

typescript
interface UserRow {
  id: number;
  name: string;
  email: string;
  active: boolean;
}

const { records } = await db.executeQuery<UserRow>(
  `SELECT id, name, email, active
     FROM users
    WHERE name = :name AND active = :active`,
  { name: "O'Reilly", active: true }
);

console.log(`Matched ${records.length} user(s)`);

Any input — including text such as "'; DROP TABLE users; --" — is passed to the server as a parameter value, never interpolated into the SQL, so it can only ever match as a literal string. For parameterless SQL, simply omit the params argument: await db.executeQuery('SELECT 1').

Reading the Query Result ​

executeQuery<R>() resolves to a PostgreSQLQueryResult<R> with three properties: records, rowCount, and fields.

typescript
import { PostgreSQLDatabase, PostgreSQLQueryResult } from 'blendsdk/postgresql';

interface UserRow {
  id: number;
  name: string;
  active: boolean;
}

const db = new PostgreSQLDatabase({
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 5432,
  database: 'appdb',
  user: 'app',
  pass: 'secret',
});

try {
  const result: PostgreSQLQueryResult<UserRow> = await db.executeQuery<UserRow>(
    'SELECT 1 AS id, :name AS name, true AS active',
    { name: 'Ada' }
  );

  console.log(result.rowCount); // 1
  console.log(result.records[0].name); // Ada
  console.log(result.fields.map((field) => field.name).join(', ')); // id, name, active
} finally {
  await db.disconnect();
}
PropertyTypeDescription
recordsR[]Rows returned by the query, typed by the generic parameter.
rowCountnumberNumber of rows returned (SELECT) or affected (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE).
fieldsFieldDef[]Column metadata reported by the driver; an empty array when no rows are returned.

Empty result sets are normalized — all three properties are empty rather than undefined:

typescript
const empty = await db.executeQuery<{ id: number }>(
  'SELECT id FROM users WHERE id = :id',
  { id: -1 }
);

console.log(empty.rowCount); // 0
console.log(empty.records); // []
console.log(empty.fields); // [] — field metadata is only present when rows are returned

Selecting Rows with Builders ​

SELECT statements can also be built with the inherited selectAll() and from() factories instead of raw SQL. selectAll(table) produces a SELECT * statement; from<T>(table) starts a column-select statement.

typescript
import { PostgreSQLDatabase } from 'blendsdk/postgresql';

interface UserRow {
  id: number;
  name: string;
  email: string;
}

const db = new PostgreSQLDatabase({
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 5432,
  database: 'appdb',
  user: 'app',
  pass: 'secret',
});

try {
  // SELECT * FROM users
  const all = await db.selectAll('users').execute();
  console.log(`All users: ${all?.rowCount ?? 0}`);

  // SELECT id, name FROM users
  const partial = await db.from<UserRow>('users').select(['id', 'name']).execute();
  console.log(`Projected columns: ${partial?.rowCount ?? 0}`);
} finally {
  await db.disconnect();
}

select() accepts '*', a column array, or an alias map that renames columns and can wrap computed expressions:

typescript
// SELECT id AS user_id, email AS contact_email FROM users
const aliased = await db
  .from<UserRow>('users')
  .select({ user_id: 'id', contact_email: 'email' })
  .execute();

Grouping Work in Transactions ​

withTransaction(fn) runs a unit of work atomically: it issues BEGIN, executes your callback, then COMMITs on success or ROLLBACKs when the callback throws. The callback receives the same database instance, so every statement executed through it — raw queries or builder operations — participates in the same transaction.

typescript
import { PostgreSQLDatabase } from 'blendsdk/postgresql';

interface BalanceRow {
  balance: string;
}

const db = new PostgreSQLDatabase({
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 5432,
  database: 'appdb',
  user: 'app',
  pass: 'secret',
});

try {
  const newBalance = await db.withTransaction(async (txDb) => {
    await txDb.executeQuery(
      'UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - :amount WHERE id = :id',
      { amount: 100, id: 1 }
    );

    // Re-read inside the transaction to enforce the overdraft rule
    const { records } = await txDb.executeQuery<BalanceRow>(
      'SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = :id',
      { id: 1 }
    );

    if (Number(records[0].balance) < 0) {
      // Throwing rolls back the whole transaction, including the debit above
      throw new Error('insufficient funds');
    }

    await txDb.executeQuery(
      'UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + :amount WHERE id = :id',
      { amount: 100, id: 2 }
    );

    return records[0].balance;
  });

  console.log(`Transfer committed — new balance: ${newBalance}`);
} catch (error) {
  if (error instanceof Error) {
    console.error(`Transfer rolled back: ${error.message}`);
  }
} finally {
  await db.disconnect();
}

Two rules keep transactions safe:

  • Use the callback argument. Statements issued through txDb use the pinned client; statements issued through db outside the callback do not.
  • Treat the instance as busy. Avoid parallel statements on the same instance and do not nest withTransaction() calls while a transaction is running.

The return value of the callback passes through unchanged, and statement builders execute inside the transaction when they are created from txDb:

typescript
const created = await db.withTransaction(async (txDb) =>
  txDb
    .insert<UserRow>('users')
    .values({ name: 'Ada Lovelace', email: 'ada@example.com' })
    .returning('*')
    .executeReturnSingle()
);

Inserting Rows ​

db.insert<T>(table) returns a fluent INSERT builder. Each key passed to .values() becomes a column and a matching :key parameter; keys you omit are left to their database defaults.

typescript
import { PostgreSQLDatabase } from 'blendsdk/postgresql';

interface UserRow {
  id?: number;
  name: string;
  email: string;
  active?: boolean;
}

const db = new PostgreSQLDatabase({
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 5432,
  database: 'appdb',
  user: 'app',
  pass: 'secret',
});

try {
  const created = await db
    .insert<UserRow>('users')
    .values({ name: 'Ada Lovelace', email: 'ada@example.com', active: true })
    .returning('*')
    .executeReturnSingle();

  if (created) {
    console.log(`Created user ${created.id} <${created.email}>`);
  }

  const inserted = await db
    .insert<UserRow>('users')
    .values({ name: 'Alan Turing', email: 'alan@example.com' })
    .executeReturnCount();

  console.log(`Inserted ${inserted} row(s)`);
} finally {
  await db.disconnect();
}

A statement ends with one of the execution methods:

TerminatorResolves with
execute()the underlying query result (records, rowCount) — useful when you need the raw result
executeReturnSingle()the first returned row (T | null) — requires a RETURNING clause
executeReturnAll()all returned rows (T[]) — requires a RETURNING clause
executeReturnCount()the number of affected rows (number)

Add .returning('*') or .returning([...columns]) before the executeReturn* terminators so the database sends the written rows back:

typescript
const result = await db
  .insert<UserRow>('users')
  .values({ name: 'Grace Hopper', email: 'grace@example.com' })
  .returning(['id', 'name'])
  .execute();

console.log(result?.rowCount); // 1

Executing an INSERT builder without calling .values() throws instead of emitting invalid SQL — see Error Handling.

Updating Rows ​

db.update<T, F>(table) builds an UPDATE with a SET clause typed by T and a WHERE clause typed by F. Each key in .values() becomes column = :v_column, and the filter compiles into parameterized WHERE conditions.

typescript
import { PostgreSQLDatabase } from 'blendsdk/postgresql';

interface UserRow {
  id?: number;
  name: string;
  email: string;
  active?: boolean;
}

interface UserFilter {
  id?: number;
  email?: string;
  active?: boolean;
  age?: number;
}

const db = new PostgreSQLDatabase({
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 5432,
  database: 'appdb',
  user: 'app',
  pass: 'secret',
});

try {
  const deactivated = await db
    .update<UserRow, UserFilter>('users')
    .values({ active: false })
    .filter({ email: 'ada@example.com' })
    .returning(['id', 'email', 'active'])
    .executeReturnSingle();

  if (deactivated) {
    console.log(`Deactivated ${deactivated.email}`);
  }

  const affected = await db
    .update<UserRow, UserFilter>('users')
    .values({ active: true })
    .filter({ active: false })
    .executeReturnCount();

  console.log(`Reactivated ${affected} user(s)`);
} finally {
  await db.disconnect();
}

Values and filter parameters occupy separate namespaces, so updating and filtering on the same column can never collide. When you need a condition beyond simple equality, .filterByExpression() compiles a callback-built condition:

typescript
// Updates every user older than 65: "UPDATE users SET active = :v_active WHERE ..."
await db
  .update<UserRow, UserFilter>('users')
  .values({ active: false })
  .filterByExpression((q) => q.where('age').greaterThan(65))
  .execute();

⚠️ An empty filter — .filter({}) or no .filter() call at all — updates every row in the table.

Deleting Rows ​

db.delete<F>(table) builds a DELETE with a WHERE clause typed by F and the same RETURNING support. It has no SET clause, so it never requires values.

typescript
import { PostgreSQLDatabase } from 'blendsdk/postgresql';

interface SessionFilter {
  user_id?: number;
  status?: string;
}

const db = new PostgreSQLDatabase({
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 5432,
  database: 'appdb',
  user: 'app',
  pass: 'secret',
});

try {
  const removed = await db
    .delete<SessionFilter>('sessions')
    .filter({ status: 'expired' })
    .executeReturnCount();

  console.log(`Removed ${removed} expired session(s)`);

  const deleted = await db
    .delete<SessionFilter>('sessions')
    .filter({ user_id: 42 })
    .returning(['user_id', 'status'])
    .executeReturnAll();

  for (const session of deleted) {
    console.log(`Removed ${session.status} session for user ${session.user_id}`);
  }
} finally {
  await db.disconnect();
}

⚠️ As with UPDATE, an omitted or empty filter deletes every row:

typescript
// Deletes EVERY row: "DELETE FROM sessions"
await db.delete<SessionFilter>('sessions').filter({}).execute();

Transforming Data with Hooks ​

beforeQuery transforms the parameter map before the SQL is compiled; afterQuery transforms the result rows before they reach your code. Chained on a statement builder, they cover the classic data-layer concerns: normalize inputs on the way in, mask sensitive fields on the way out.

typescript
import { PostgreSQLDatabase } from 'blendsdk/postgresql';

interface UserRow {
  id?: number;
  name: string;
  email: string;
  password_hash?: string;
}

const db = new PostgreSQLDatabase({
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 5432,
  database: 'appdb',
  user: 'app',
  pass: 'secret',
});

try {
  const created = await db
    .insert<UserRow>('users')
    .values({ name: 'Grace Hopper', email: 'GRACE@EXAMPLE.COM', password_hash: 'plain-secret' })
    .beforeQuery((params) => {
      const transformed = { ...params };
      if (typeof transformed.email === 'string') {
        transformed.email = transformed.email.toLowerCase();
      }
      if (typeof transformed.password_hash === 'string') {
        transformed.password_hash = `hash(${transformed.password_hash})`;
      }
      return transformed;
    })
    .afterQuery((records) =>
      records.map((record) => {
        const safe = { ...record };
        delete safe.password_hash;
        return safe;
      })
    )
    .returning('*')
    .executeReturnSingle();

  if (created) {
    console.log(`Stored ${created.email} — password hash hidden by afterQuery`);
  }
} finally {
  await db.disconnect();
}

The same transforms can be supplied per call through executeQuery() options:

typescript
const { records } = await db.executeQuery<UserRow>(
  'SELECT id, name, email FROM users WHERE email = :email',
  { email: 'GRACE@EXAMPLE.COM' },
  {
    beforeQuery: (params) => ({ ...params, email: 'grace@example.com' }),
    afterQuery: (rows) => rows.map((row) => ({ ...row, name: row.name.toUpperCase() })),
  }
);

A hook that throws rejects the operation exactly like a query error — inside a transaction it triggers the automatic rollback.

Closing the Connection ​

disconnect() sets the adapter's shutdown guard, drains the pool, and releases all clients. Call it when the application shuts down — typically in a finally block.

typescript
import { PostgreSQLDatabase } from 'blendsdk/postgresql';

const db = new PostgreSQLDatabase({
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 5432,
  database: 'appdb',
  user: 'app',
  pass: 'secret',
});

await db.executeQuery('SELECT 1');

// Graceful close with a 5-second ceiling (default: 10000 ms)
await db.disconnect(5000);
console.log('Pool closed');

// The shutdown guard rejects any further work
try {
  await db.executeQuery('SELECT 1');
} catch (error) {
  if (error instanceof Error) {
    console.error(error.message); // Cannot execute query: database is shutting down
  }
}
  • If draining takes longer than the timeout, the remaining clients are force-released — which may interrupt in-flight queries — and disconnect() still resolves.
  • disconnect() is safe on an instance that never executed a query.

For standalone processes — and only those — the adapter can handle SIGINT/SIGTERM itself:

typescript
const db = new PostgreSQLDatabase({
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 5432,
  database: 'appdb',
  user: 'app',
  pass: 'secret',
  enableGracefulShutdown: true, // registers SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers — standalone processes only
});

⚠️ Warning: do NOT enable enableGracefulShutdown when the database is managed by a WebApplication from blendsdk/webafx, which has its own SIGTERM/SIGINT handling. Registering both causes signal handler conflicts and unpredictable shutdown behavior.

Configuration ​

All configuration is passed as a single PostgreSQLConfig object to the constructor. It extends DatabaseConfig from blendsdk/dbcore — the connection settings shared across the BlendSDK data stack — with PostgreSQL-specific pool tuning and lifecycle options. The constructor performs no validation: wrong credentials or an unreachable server surface as a rejected query, not as a construction error.

Connection Options ​

OptionTypeDefaultDescription
hoststring'localhost' (pg driver default)Hostname of the PostgreSQL server.
portnumber | string5432 (pg driver default)Server port. Numeric strings are coerced with Number() during construction.
databasestring—Name of the database to connect to.
userstring—Database role used for authentication.
passstring—Password; forwarded to the driver as its password option.

Pool and Lifecycle Options ​

OptionTypeDefaultDescription
poolConfigPoolConfigundefined (pg driver defaults apply)Optional tuning of the underlying pg.Pool; may be provided partially or omitted entirely.
poolConfig.maxnumber10Maximum number of clients in the pool.
poolConfig.idleTimeoutMillisnumber30000Milliseconds a client may sit idle before it is closed.
poolConfig.connectionTimeoutMillisnumber0 (no timeout)Milliseconds to wait for a new client to connect before timing out.
enableGracefulShutdownbooleanfalseWhen true, registers SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers that close the pool and exit the process.

⚠️ Do not enable enableGracefulShutdown when a WebApplication from blendsdk/webafx manages the database lifecycle — the framework already handles SIGTERM/SIGINT, and two sets of signal handlers conflict. See Closing the Connection.

Complete Configuration ​

typescript
import { PostgreSQLConfig, PostgreSQLDatabase } from 'blendsdk/postgresql';

const config: PostgreSQLConfig = {
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 5432,
  database: 'appdb',
  user: 'app',
  pass: 'secret',
  poolConfig: {
    max: 20,
    idleTimeoutMillis: 60000,
    connectionTimeoutMillis: 5000,
  },
  enableGracefulShutdown: false,
};

const db = new PostgreSQLDatabase(config);

try {
  const { rowCount } = await db.executeQuery('SELECT 1');
  console.log(`Query succeeded (${rowCount} row)`);
} finally {
  await db.disconnect();
}

Environment-Based Configuration ​

A common pattern is to build the configuration object from environment variables:

typescript
const config: PostgreSQLConfig = {
  host: process.env.PGHOST ?? 'localhost',
  port: Number(process.env.PGPORT ?? 5432),
  database: process.env.PGDATABASE ?? 'appdb',
  user: process.env.PGUSER ?? 'app',
  pass: process.env.PGPASSWORD ?? 'secret',
};

Error Handling ​

Failures come in two families:

  1. Adapter errors — plain Error instances raised by the package itself (shutdown guards and builder validation). There are no custom error classes to instanceof; match them by their exact message when you need to.
  2. Driver errors — failures propagated unchanged from the pg driver: connection problems, invalid SQL, constraint violations. They carry PostgreSQL diagnostics such as the SQLSTATE code.

Adapter Errors ​

MessageRaised when
Cannot execute query: database is shutting downexecuteQuery() — or any statement execution — is called after disconnect() has begun.
Cannot start transaction: database is shutting downwithTransaction() is called after disconnect() has begun.
No database connection available.Internal guard: a pooled client could not be acquired for an atomic query.
Cannot build INSERT statement for table "<name>": no values provided. Call .values() with at least one column before executing.An INSERT builder is executed without .values().
Cannot build UPDATE statement for table "<name>": no values provided. Call .values() with at least one column before executing.An UPDATE builder is executed without .values().

Driver Errors ​

Driver errors are Error instances with additional diagnostics. The reliable way to branch on a specific failure is the SQLSTATE code, not the message text.

PropertyTypeDescription
messagestringHuman-readable error text from PostgreSQL.
codestringSQLSTATE code — the stable identifier for the failure class.
detailstring | undefinedAdditional detail, e.g. which key already exists.
constraintstring | undefinedName of the violated constraint, when applicable.
tablestring | undefinedTable involved, when applicable.

Common SQLSTATE codes you will meet early:

CodeNameMeaning
23505unique_violationDuplicate value for a unique index or primary key.
23503foreign_key_violationA referenced row is missing, or a row is still referenced.
23502not_null_violationNULL inserted into a NOT NULL column.
42P01undefined_tableThe table does not exist.
42601syntax_errorThe SQL statement could not be parsed.

Recovery Guarantees ​

  • Failed queries release their client. The connection returns to the pool in a finally block; the instance stays usable after an error.
  • Failed transactions roll back and rethrow. withTransaction() attempts ROLLBACK, then rethrows the original error; the client is always released.
  • Hook failures propagate. A throw inside beforeQuery or afterQuery rejects the operation like a query error and rolls back an enclosing transaction.
  • Cleanup failures never mask the original error. Problems during rollback or client release are logged via console.error; the error you catch is the one that caused the failure.
  • disconnect() is timeout-protected. After the timeout (default 10 000 ms) remaining clients are force-released and disconnect() resolves; only a pool-end failure before the timeout is rethrown.

Complete Example ​

The following example inserts a user and handles both error families: a unique-constraint violation from the driver and any other failure.

typescript
import { PostgreSQLDatabase } from 'blendsdk/postgresql';

interface UserRow {
  id?: number;
  name: string;
  email: string;
}

interface PgError extends Error {
  code?: string;
  constraint?: string;
}

function isPgError(error: unknown): error is PgError {
  if (!(error instanceof Error)) {
    return false;
  }
  const candidate: Partial<PgError> = error;
  return typeof candidate.code === 'string';
}

const db = new PostgreSQLDatabase({
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 5432,
  database: 'appdb',
  user: 'app',
  pass: 'secret',
});

try {
  await db
    .insert<UserRow>('users')
    .values({ name: 'Ada Lovelace', email: 'ada@example.com' })
    .execute();
  console.log('Inserted');
} catch (error) {
  if (isPgError(error) && error.code === '23505') {
    console.warn(`Duplicate rejected by constraint "${error.constraint}"`);
  } else if (error instanceof Error) {
    console.error(`Database operation failed: ${error.message}`);
  } else {
    console.error('Database operation failed with a non-Error value:', error);
  }
} finally {
  await db.disconnect();
}

postgresql Advanced Patterns ​

This document collects end-to-end solutions that combine the building blocks introduced in Core Concepts: transactions, statement builders, query hooks, compiled expressions, and lifecycle management. Each section presents a concrete production problem — checkout flows, ingestion pipelines, job queues, reporting, service lifecycle — with a complete implementation, the reasoning behind the pattern, and the constraints to keep in mind.

The patterns covered are:

  • Transactional Units of Work — multiple builders and raw SQL in one all-or-nothing transaction
  • Reusable Hook Pipelines — composable beforeQuery/afterQuery policies shared across every write and read path
  • Conditional Filters with the Expression API — optional, grouped, injection-safe predicates for maintenance jobs and reads
  • Idempotent Writes: Check-then-Act and Native Upserts — exactly-one-row semantics for retried or duplicated input
  • Job Claiming with SKIP LOCKED — a work queue on top of the jobs table with guarded updates and stall recovery
  • Report Queries with Result Shaping — named-parameter aggregation shaped at the result boundary
  • Service Lifecycle and Pool Management — pool sizing, fail-fast startup, and deterministic shutdown

All examples assume the referenced tables exist on the server; each interface models the columns it uses. Import every symbol you use — all symbols shown below are public exports of blendsdk/postgresql (or, where noted, of blendsdk/expression).

Transactional Units of Work ​

When to use it ​

  • Two or more writes that must succeed or fail as a group — order placement, funds transfer, provisioning.
  • A write that must be guarded by a read — checking stock, balances, or quotas before mutating.
  • Any flow where a partially applied change would corrupt business state and manual BEGIN/COMMIT orchestration would be error-prone.

The pattern ​

withTransaction() pins one pooled client and runs BEGIN → work → COMMIT, rolling back and rethrowing when the callback throws. Every builder call on the callback's txDb handle — and every raw executeQuery — joins the same server-side transaction. The example below composes an INSERT builder, a locking SELECT, an UPDATE builder, and a second INSERT builder into a single checkout operation.

typescript
import { PostgreSQLConfig, PostgreSQLDatabase } from 'blendsdk/postgresql';

interface OrderRow {
  id?: number;
  user_id: number;
  status: string;
  total: string;
}

interface OrderItemRow {
  id?: number;
  order_id: number;
  product_id: number;
  quantity: number;
  unit_price: string;
}

interface ProductRow {
  id?: number;
  name: string;
  stock: number;
  price: string;
}

interface CartLine {
  productId: number;
  quantity: number;
}

class InsufficientStockError extends Error {
  public readonly productId: number;
  public readonly available: number;
  public readonly requested: number;

  constructor(productId: number, available: number, requested: number) {
    super(`Product ${productId}: requested ${requested}, only ${available} in stock`);
    this.name = 'InsufficientStockError';
    this.productId = productId;
    this.available = available;
    this.requested = requested;
  }
}

const config: PostgreSQLConfig = {
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 5432,
  database: 'shop',
  user: 'app',
  pass: 'secret',
};

const db = new PostgreSQLDatabase(config);

async function placeOrder(userId: number, lines: CartLine[]): Promise<number> {
  // Deterministic lock ordering prevents deadlocks between concurrent checkouts
  const sortedLines = [...lines].sort((a, b) => a.productId - b.productId);

  return db.withTransaction(async (txDb) => {
    // 1. Create the order header; RETURNING provides the generated id
    const order = await txDb
      .insert<OrderRow>('orders')
      .values({ user_id: userId, status: 'pending', total: '0.00' })
      .returning(['id'])
      .executeReturnSingle();

    if (!order?.id) {
      throw new Error('Order insert did not return an id');
    }

    let total = 0;

    for (const line of sortedLines) {
      // 2. Lock the product row for the rest of the transaction
      const { records } = await txDb.executeQuery<ProductRow>(
        `SELECT id, name, stock, price
           FROM products
          WHERE id = :id
          FOR UPDATE`,
        { id: line.productId }
      );

      const product = records[0];
      if (!product) {
        throw new Error(`Unknown product: ${line.productId}`);
      }
      if (product.stock < line.quantity) {
        throw new InsufficientStockError(line.productId, product.stock, line.quantity);
      }

      total += Number(product.price) * line.quantity;

      // 3. Decrement stock and record the line item
      await txDb
        .update<ProductRow, { id?: number }>('products')
        .values({ stock: product.stock - line.quantity })
        .filter({ id: line.productId })
        .execute();

      await txDb
        .insert<OrderItemRow>('order_items')
        .values({
          order_id: order.id,
          product_id: line.productId,
          quantity: line.quantity,
          unit_price: product.price,
        })
        .execute();
    }

    // 4. Finalize the total; any failure above rolls back everything
    await txDb
      .update<OrderRow, { id?: number }>('orders')
      .values({ total: total.toFixed(2) })
      .filter({ id: order.id })
      .execute();

    return order.id;
  });
}

try {
  const orderId = await placeOrder(42, [
    { productId: 7, quantity: 2 },
    { productId: 3, quantity: 1 },
  ]);
  console.log(`Order ${orderId} placed successfully`);
} catch (error) {
  if (error instanceof InsufficientStockError) {
    console.error(`Checkout rejected: ${error.message}`);
  } else {
    throw error;
  }
} finally {
  await db.disconnect();
}

Each builder chain compiles to parameterized SQL the named-parameter compiler can bind safely:

typescript
// insert<OrderRow>('orders').values({...}).returning(['id'])
// → INSERT INTO orders (user_id, status, total) VALUES (:user_id, :status, :total) RETURNING id

// update<ProductRow, ...>('products').values({ stock }).filter({ id })
// → UPDATE products SET stock = :v_stock WHERE id = :p1

// update<OrderRow, ...>('orders').values({ total }).filter({ id })
// → UPDATE orders SET total = :v_total WHERE id = :p1

Why this pattern is valuable ​

  • Atomicity without manual bookkeeping. BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, and client release are handled for you; an exception anywhere in the flow — a failed query, a domain rule violation, a bug — removes every write, including the order row whose id was already returned to your code.
  • Consistency through client pinning. All statements run on one client, so the FOR UPDATE lock taken by the SELECT is still held by the later UPDATE. This closes the oversell race that a read-then-write across pooled connections would leave open.
  • Fewer round trips. RETURNING delivers generated ids and affected rows in the same statement, no follow-up SELECT needed.

Caveats and performance notes ​

  • The instance is busy during a transaction. transactionClient is pinned, so use only the txDb handle inside the callback, never fire concurrent queries on the same instance, and never start a nested withTransaction() — it would join the outer transaction's client unintentionally.
  • Keep transactions short. Locks live until commit; long transactions block other writers. Do validation, HTTP calls, and computation outside the transaction and touch the database only for the unit of work itself.
  • Sort lock acquisition. Acquiring row locks in a deterministic order (here: ascending product ids) prevents deadlock cycles between concurrent transactions.
  • A failed transaction does not poison the instance. The client is always released in a finally block, and the original error is the one you see — a failing rollback is logged, not rethrown over it.

Reusable Hook Pipelines ​

When to use it ​

  • The same normalization, hashing, or sanitization rules apply to every write of a table, and repeating them inline on each chain invites omissions.
  • Outputs must be shielded — passwords and tokens removed, decimals parsed, dates formatted — before records reach application code.
  • You want data-protection policy expressed as small, testable functions instead of scattered inline callbacks.

The pattern ​

Compose hook factories into a per-resource policy, then let repository functions own the only chains that touch the table. beforeQuery transforms the parameter map (values only — keys are fixed by the statement), and afterQuery transforms the returned rows.

typescript
import { createHash } from 'node:crypto';
import { PostgreSQLConfig, PostgreSQLDatabase } from 'blendsdk/postgresql';

type ParamMap = Record<string, unknown>;
type ParamHook = (params: ParamMap) => ParamMap;
type RecordHook<T> = (records: T[]) => T[];

interface UserRow {
  id?: number;
  name: string;
  email: string;
  password_hash?: string;
}

interface NewUser {
  name: string;
  email: string;
  password_hash: string;
}

function composeParamHooks(...hooks: ParamHook[]): ParamHook {
  return (params) => hooks.reduce((current, hook) => hook(current), params);
}

// --- Reusable parameter hooks ----------------------------------------------

const trimStrings: ParamHook = (params) => {
  const next: ParamMap = {};
  for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(params)) {
    next[key] = typeof value === 'string' && !key.includes('password') ? value.trim() : value;
  }
  return next;
};

const canonicalizeEmail: ParamHook = (params) => {
  const next = { ...params };
  for (const key of ['email', 'v_email']) {
    const value = next[key];
    if (typeof value === 'string') {
      next[key] = value.toLowerCase();
    }
  }
  return next;
};

const digestPassword: ParamHook = (params) => {
  const next = { ...params };
  for (const key of ['password_hash', 'v_password_hash']) {
    const value = next[key];
    if (typeof value === 'string') {
      next[key] = createHash('sha256').update(value).digest('hex');
    }
  }
  return next;
};

// --- Reusable record hooks --------------------------------------------------

const shieldUserSecrets: RecordHook<UserRow> = (records) =>
  records.map((record) => {
    const safe = { ...record };
    delete safe.password_hash;
    return safe;
  });

// --- Repository functions: the only chains that touch the table -------------

const userWritePolicy = composeParamHooks(trimStrings, canonicalizeEmail, digestPassword);

async function createUser(db: PostgreSQLDatabase, values: NewUser): Promise<UserRow | null> {
  return db
    .insert<UserRow>('users')
    .values(values)
    .beforeQuery(userWritePolicy)
    .afterQuery(shieldUserSecrets)
    .returning('*')
    .executeReturnSingle();
}

async function renameUser(
  db: PostgreSQLDatabase,
  id: number,
  values: { name: string; email: string }
): Promise<UserRow | null> {
  return db
    .update<UserRow, { id?: number }>('users')
    .values(values)
    .filter({ id })
    .beforeQuery(userWritePolicy)
    .afterQuery(shieldUserSecrets)
    .returning('*')
    .executeReturnSingle();
}

const config: PostgreSQLConfig = {
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 5432,
  database: 'shop',
  user: 'app',
  pass: 'secret',
};

const db = new PostgreSQLDatabase(config);

try {
  const created = await createUser(db, {
    name: '  Ada Lovelace  ',
    email: 'ADA@EXAMPLE.COM',
    password_hash: 'correct horse battery staple',
  });

  if (created?.id) {
    console.log(`Created ${created.name} <${created.email}>`);

    const renamed = await renameUser(db, created.id, {
      name: 'Ada Byron',
      email: 'ada.byron@EXAMPLE.COM',
    });

    if (renamed) {
      console.log(`Renamed to ${renamed.name} <${renamed.email}>`);
    }
  }
} finally {
  await db.disconnect();
}

The hook pipeline runs identically for INSERT and UPDATE, even though the parameter namespaces differ — that difference is absorbed once, in the hook factories:

typescript
// INSERT parameters (column names):
//   { name: '  Ada Lovelace  ', email: 'ADA@EXAMPLE.COM', password_hash: 'correct horse...' }
// → { name: 'Ada Lovelace', email: 'ada@example.com', password_hash: 'e3b0c442...' }

// UPDATE parameters (values are v_-prefixed, filters are p1…pN):
//   { v_name: 'Ada Byron', v_email: 'ada.byron@EXAMPLE.COM', p1: 1 }
// → { v_name: 'Ada Byron', v_email: 'ada.byron@example.com', p1: 1 }

Before this pattern, every call site re-implemented the policy inline — one omission leaks a plaintext secret or stores an unnormalized email:

typescript
// Before: policy duplicated at every call site
await db
  .insert<UserRow>('users')
  .values({ name, email, password_hash })
  .beforeQuery((params) => {
    const next = { ...params };
    if (typeof next.email === 'string') next.email = next.email.toLowerCase();
    return next; // ← hashing forgotten on this call site
  });

// After: one repository function owns the policy for the table
await createUser(db, { name: 'Ada Lovelace', email: 'ADA@EXAMPLE.COM', password_hash: 'secret' });

Why this pattern is valuable ​

  • One choke point per resource. Every write path flows through userWritePolicy; a new rule (audit timestamps, PII redaction) is added in one place and applies everywhere instantly.
  • Testable, pure functions. Each hook is a plain ParamMap → ParamMap or T[] → T[] function that can be unit-tested without a database.
  • Safe-by-default reads. shieldUserSecrets guarantees password_hash never leaves the repository layer, even if a caller forgets to project columns.

Caveats and performance notes ​

  • Transform values, not keys. Placeholders are generated from the keys you pass to .values() / .filter(); renaming or deleting a key inside a hook leaves its placeholder unbound and breaks compilation. Handle both email and v_email spellings instead of renaming.
